questions.prompt: A request calls another service and a database. Which telemetry structure represents these related operations?

choices.text: A trace composed of related spans.
One global counter used as a unique request identifier.
A log severity level that replaces all timing data.
An unrelated trace ID generated for every child operation.

questions.explanation: A trace links timed operations through spans. Counters aggregate activity, and unrelated IDs prevent reconstructing one operation.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry traces
sources.claim: A trace records an operation across spans; spans carry timing, identifiers, attributes and parent-child relationships.

questions.prompt: Two instrumented services produce unrelated traces for one request. What boundary should be checked first?

choices.text: Whether the downstream service starts a new root trace instead of continuing context.
Whether both services drop incoming trace headers after accepting the request.
Whether the client propagator omits context on outgoing calls.
Trace-context injection and extraction across the call.

questions.explanation: Distributed tracing needs outgoing context injection and incoming extraction. Dropped headers, omitted propagation or starting an unrelated root trace break the link between service operations.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry context propagation
sources.claim: Injecting and extracting trace context links service spans; baggage propagates arbitrary values and should not contain sensitive credentials.

questions.prompt: A request counter adds a unique user-generated URL to every measurement. What risk should the telemetry design consider?

choices.text: The counter changes into a guaranteed database transaction log.
Unique labels make storage and aggregation cost independent of traffic.
Too many attribute combinations and cardinality overflow.
Every attribute combination becomes one distributed trace automatically.

questions.explanation: High-cardinality labels create many time series and can hit limits. They do not become traces or eliminate telemetry costs.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry metrics
sources.claim: Metrics aggregate runtime measurements; histograms summarize distributions and high-cardinality attribute combinations can exceed SDK cardinality limits.

questions.prompt: A structured log records a failed database call. Which fields help connect it to the relevant request trace?

choices.text: Only the aggregate number of errors observed during that time window.
TraceId and SpanId.
Only the human-readable severity string.
Only the deployment’s public hostname.

questions.explanation: Trace and span IDs identify the related operation. Severity, host and aggregate counts do not uniquely locate that request work.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry logs
sources.claim: OpenTelemetry logs include body and severity along with optional trace and span IDs for correlating events with request work.

questions.prompt: A service creates two child operations inside one trace. Which identity relationship is appropriate?

choices.text: Share the trace ID but use distinct span IDs.
Use one span ID for every operation regardless of parent.
Give every child an unrelated trace ID to join the parent.
Replace trace identity with a request-count total.

questions.explanation: The trace ID groups the operation; each span ID identifies a specific unit of work. Unrelated traces and aggregate totals lose the relationship.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry traces
sources.claim: Trace spans have a shared trace identity and individual span identity.

questions.prompt: A developer puts an API secret in trace baggage for troubleshooting. What is the problem?

choices.text: Baggage always encrypts each value for only one recipient.
The value cannot leave the originating process under any propagator.
Using baggage automatically revokes the original API secret.
Baggage can propagate or be logged beyond the intended trust boundary.

questions.explanation: Baggage is propagated context, not secret storage. It may reach downstream systems and logs, and does not encrypt or revoke credentials by itself.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry context propagation
sources.claim: Baggage propagates key-value pairs and can disclose data across service boundaries.

questions.prompt: Which tracing statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A span represents a timed unit of work.
Parent-child relationships help reconstruct a distributed operation.
Every span in one trace must have the same span identifier.
A trace is only an aggregate count with no per-operation timing.
A child must use an unrelated trace ID to remain linked to its parent.

questions.explanation: A is correct: Its start and end describe one operation. B is correct: Related spans form the trace structure. C is incorrect: Spans have distinct IDs within the shared trace. D is incorrect: Traces retain individual operation structure. E is incorrect: Shared trace context connects the operations.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry traces
sources.claim: A trace records an operation across spans; spans carry timing, identifiers, attributes and parent-child relationships.

questions.prompt: Which propagation choices are appropriate? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Extract incoming context when continuing a distributed operation.
Avoid sensitive credentials or personal data in baggage.
Treat received trace headers as proof of authentication.
Propagate every internal baggage value to all external services without review.
Inject trace context into outgoing requests.

questions.explanation: A is correct: It establishes the relationship to the upstream trace. B is correct: Baggage can cross trust boundaries and be logged. C is incorrect: Trace context is correlation data, not an authorization credential. D is incorrect: Outgoing context can expose sensitive details. E is correct: The downstream service needs the caller’s context.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry context propagation
sources.claim: Injecting and extracting trace context links service spans; baggage propagates arbitrary values and should not contain sensitive credentials.

questions.prompt: Which metric-design statements hold? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A monotonically increasing Counter is ideal for a value that rises and falls.
Adding unique identifiers has no effect on the number of metric series.
Every metric measurement retains a complete parent-child request trace.
Histograms can summarize distributions such as request latency.
Attribute combinations contribute to metric cardinality.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: An UpDownCounter fits accumulations that can decrease. B is incorrect: Unique values increase distinct combinations. C is incorrect: Metrics aggregate values rather than preserve all trace structure. D is correct: They aggregate observed values into statistical summaries. E is correct: Distinct combinations create distinct aggregation dimensions.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry metrics
sources.claim: Metrics aggregate runtime measurements; histograms summarize distributions and high-cardinality attribute combinations can exceed SDK cardinality limits.

questions.prompt: Which logging statements match the OpenTelemetry model? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Every log record must have identical timestamp and observed timestamp.
Matching log severity is sufficient to correlate concurrent requests uniquely.
A log body records the event content.
Severity conveys the event’s importance level.
Trace and span identifiers support correlation with request operations.

questions.explanation: A is incorrect: Occurrence and observation times can differ. B is incorrect: Many requests produce logs at the same level. C is correct: Body contains the log record’s message or structured data. D is correct: Severity text and number classify the log. E is correct: They can connect logs to traces.

sources.title: OpenTelemetry logs
sources.claim: OpenTelemetry logs include body and severity along with optional trace and span IDs for correlating events with request work.
